title: Statistics for economics (CBSE 11)
examples: How do we choose the right way to collect data for an economy?
What is the difference between a simple average and a weighted average?
Can you show me an example of how an index number is calculated?

explain.say: Today we learn about using statistics in economics.

items: Primary data: collected directly by you.
Secondary data: already collected by others.

explain.say: Primary data means gathering information yourself for a study.
Secondary data comes from reports already published by other groups.
Measures help us summarize large amounts of collected numbers simply.
Index numbers track changes in a group of related items over time.
For instance, the Consumer Price Index tracks cost of living changes.

faq.q: What is the difference between primary and secondary data?
faq.a: Primary data is information you collect yourself directly for your specific research goal. Secondary data is information that someone else has already collected and published for a different purpose.
asks: Where do I get my own data?
Is using government reports always secondary data?

faq.q: When should I use the median instead of the mean?
faq.a: You should use the median when your data has extreme outliers, like very high or very low values. The median is less affected by these extreme points than the mean.
asks: Does the mean work well with salaries?
What if some numbers are way out of place?

faq.q: How is an index number different from a simple average?
faq.a: An index number measures the relative change of a group of items compared to a base period. A simple average just calculates the typical value across all items.
asks: Is an index number just a fancy average?

faq.q: Can I use data from different years in the same index?
faq.a: Yes, index numbers are specifically designed to compare values across different time periods. This shows trends over time.
asks: Does the index need a starting point?
How do I compare Year 2 to Year 1?

faq.q: What is a good source for secondary economic data?
faq.a: Reputable sources include national statistical offices or international bodies like the World Bank. Always check the source's credibility.

facts: Primary data collection methods include surveys and direct observation.
The mean, median, and mode are measures of central tendency.
Index numbers track the change in price or quantity of goods.
The Consumer Price Index measures the average change in prices paid by urban consumers.

quiz.say: A researcher interviews 50 local shop owners about rent increases.
quiz.why: Because the researcher collected the information directly from the shop owners for this specific study, it is primary data.

wrong.0: This is wrong because secondary data means someone else already collected the information for you.
wrong.1: This is wrong because a measure is a summary calculation, not the raw data source.
wrong.2: This is wrong because an index number tracks change over time, not the initial collection of data.

quiz.say: If the salaries are 20, 25, 30, 35, and 200, what is the best measure of central tendency?
quiz.why: The median is the middle value, which is 30, because the very high salary of 200 would pull the mean up unfairly.

wrong.1: The mean would be pulled too high by the single very large salary of 200.
wrong.2: The mode is only useful if a number repeats, and no number repeats here.
wrong.3: The range only shows the spread, not the typical center value.

quiz.say: If the price of petrol rose from 100 units to 120 units, what is the index number change?
quiz.why: Index numbers compare the new value to the old value, so you divide the new price by the old price.

wrong.1: Subtracting gives you the absolute change, not the relative index change.
wrong.2: You must always put the new value in the numerator for the correct index calculation.
wrong.3: Adding the values gives a total, which is not how relative price changes are measured.
